big_idea: The LOONIE = $1. The TOONIE = $2. They are CANADIAN coins.
learning_intention: We are learning to identify the loonie and toonie.
student_learning_goal: I can identify the loonie and toonie.
success_criteria: I can NAME loonie and toonie.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Penny the Penguin — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Penny the Penguin: Friends — meet two SPECIAL CANADIAN coins! The LOONIE = $1. The TOONIE = $2! Penny opens: 'COUNT the VALUE, not the COINS!' (Class echoes.)
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Penny the Penguin puppet. 'Shoppers — yesterday we met 4 coins. Today we add 2 BIG coins — the LOONIE and the TOONIE!'

Reveal the loonie. 'LOONIE. GOLD coloured. ONE side shows the LOON BIRD — Canada's bird. Loonie = $1.00 = 100¢!'

Reveal the toonie. 'TOONIE. TWO colours — silver inside, gold ring outside. POLAR BEAR on the back. Toonie = $2.00 = 200¢!'

'Penny says — LOONIE has the LOON. TOONIE = TWO loonies = $2!'

Demo. 'I have 1 loonie. Plus 1 loonie. = 2 loonies = $2 = 1 TOONIE!'

Now show all 6 coins together (nickel, dime, quarter, 50¢, loonie, toonie). 'Sort by VALUE!'

Sorted: nickel (5¢) → dime (10¢) → quarter (25¢) → 50¢ → loonie ($1) → toonie ($2).

'Penny says — Canadian coins are SPECIAL. Loonie has a loon. Toonie has a polar bear!'

Now each pair gets the Coin Cards (now 30 — added 5 loonies + 5 toonies). They sort all 30 by name.

'Penny says — count loonies + toonies — they're worth MORE than other coins!'

steps.instruction: Hand out Coin Cards. Pairs sort by NAME (6 piles now).
Find loonie and toonie in each pile.
Help by pointing to value chart.

INVENT-AND-COMPARE: Pairs prove '1 toonie = 2 loonies' three different ways — stack the coins, line them up side-by-side, count by 1s. Class compares which is most convincing. Cite Mix & Sarama (2008) on monetary unit equivalence — different compositions of the same VALUE.
steps.teacher_prompt: Penny: 'Same VALUE, different ways. The TOTAL is what matters, not how many coins make it.'

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Five signals: names; values; finds loonie/toonie; relates; consistency.

discussion_prompts: What animal is on the loonie?
consolidation.exit_routine: Penny + Cassie refrain — class chants 3x: 'COUNT the VALUE, not the COINS!' Then Cassie's echo: 'Same VALUE, different ways!' Each child writes ONE coin name + value on a sticky.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says LOONIE is just bigger than dime — repairing the value-jump trap at Grade 1
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
Grade 1 children frequently confuse coin name and coin VALUE — they can name 'loonie' or 'toonie' but cannot say its purchasing value. Mix & Levine (2011, 'Coin Value Learning in Young Children') and Carpenter & Moser CGI work on unit composition both place the value-naming gap as the gateway to all later money work; without it, Lessons 3-5 cannot ground in real value reasoning.

Yesterday introduced coin recognition (Lesson 1). Today we pin VALUE to each coin name. Tomorrow we introduce bills (Lesson 3) and Day 4 compares values across denominations.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Sort activity. Child puts loonie in same pile as quarter.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Penny asks — what colour is loonie? GOLD. Quarter is SILVER. Different!'

Probe. 'Loonie = $1 = 100 cents! Quarter = 25 cents. Loonie is FOUR times more!'

Generalise. 'Penny says — loonie and toonie are GOLD. Coins under $1 are SILVER. Different colours, big jump in value.'

If still mixed: stack 4 quarters = $1 = 1 loonie. 'See the jump!'
common_misconceptions: All coins same. (Repair: gold vs silver.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child names loonie but doesn't say value: drill 100¢ = $1 using a quarter-stack (4 quarters → 1 loonie), Penny models the count.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child cannot name coin yet: return to Lesson 1 colour/animal naming for that coin only, then layer value on top.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child says toonie = '2 dollars' but doesn't know it equals two loonies: physical exchange — child swaps one toonie for two loonies on Cassie's tray and counts both as $2.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of F1.1 dollar coins.

parts_outline.task: Identify loonie and toonie among 6 coins.
Show how many LOONIES make 1 TOONIE.
